rows.why: Two of the examples (2d and 1d0h0m0s0ms) only pass if `d` is accepted as a unit, which is the question item 1 asks. Item 1 picks accepting `d`. The zero-component rows also fit item 7, which agrees too, but the day unit is what most sets this scenario apart.

Item 3 asks whether whitespace around components is allowed. The scenario expects leading and trailing whitespace to be ignored ("  45m\n" gives 2700000), but the pick rejects all whitespace, including ` 1s`.

The scenario lists many kinds of bad input, and item 4 covers the most rows: 1.5h, -3s, +3s and 3S. Its pick rejects all of them, as expected. Items 3, 5 and 8 cover other rows and also agree. One row clashes with another item: `05s` must be rejected here, but item 7's pick accepts leading zeros.
No item asks whether one count can be larger than the next unit up (90m instead of 1h30m) when parsing. Item 2 is about the order of units and item 10 is about formatting.
Item 2 asks about out-of-order and repeated units. Its pick rejects `30m1h` and `1h1h`, which is what the scenario expects.
Item 6 asks for the largest duration that can be parsed. Its pick caps the total at 2^53-1 ms, so 9007199254740991 parses.
The same cap question as S6. Item 6's pick returns an error above 2^53-1 or on arithmetic overflow, which covers both examples.

Item 10 asks how format_duration chooses a form. The scenario expects one breakdown from the largest unit down (90000 gives `1m30s`, 5400000 gives `1h30m`). The pick chooses the shortest string, so it prints `90s` and `90m`. The row for 0 also clashes with item 9, which prints `0s` instead of `0ms`.

The output form depends on item 10's rule. Under the shortest-string pick, `104249991d8h59m991ms` (20 characters) loses to shorter candidates of 18 characters, such as `150119987579m991ms`. So the pick does not give the expected text.
No item asks whether formatting and then parsing gives back the same number.

Item 11 asks what format_duration does above the maximum. Its pick returns a MillisecondsOutOfRange error for anything above 2^53-1, which covers both examples. The pick names the error variant but not its message, so the match on the word "milliseconds" is inferred from that name.
